title: Bank shares drop as John Healey prepares to raise taxes on the banking sector in the budget – business live
text:
Introduction: John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.
Britain’s banks may be ‘part of the jewel’ in the UK economic crown, as chancellor John Healey put it yesterday, but that won’t protect them from being hit in this month’s budget.
John Healey is poised to raise the tax take from Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget, the Guardian understands, as the chancellor looks to fix the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East.
As my colleagues HeatherStewart, Jessica Elgot and Kalyeena Makortoffreported last night, Healey has decided to tap the financial sector for additional revenue.
One option understood to be under discussion – reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt – would raise upwards of £2bn a year.
Industry figures believe that will probably mean raising the surcharge back to 8%, from 3% at present, to help bolster the government’s fiscal headroom (which has been eroded by the jump in borrowing costs this year).
News of the looming tax raid came hours after Healey praised the banks as crucial to supporting economic growth, telling reporters:
“People too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.”
Banks sound resigned to being shorn at the budget, but they’re not happy about it.
Banking sector trade body, UKFinance, warned that “further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government’s ambition to deliver growth in every postcode”.
Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be “on the menu” at the budget….
Higher taxes on banks could have an impact on the FTSE100 since the banking sector makes up nearly 20% of the UK blue chip shares index, says Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.
The UK’s banking sector has been extremely resilient this year and has performed positively, for example Lloyds Banking Group is higher by 20% in the past 12 months. The risk is that downward pressure will now build, and this will dim the attractiveness of the entire index.
We will need to wait for the Budget to get the details of this tax, afterall, this is the Labour Party and they are well known for their U-turns. The Chancellor may need to water down plans for a tax if he wants to avoid denting both the economy and the FTSE 100.
Back in Bangkok, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva has warned that the risks of artificial intelligence may exceed its opportunities if no adequate safeguards and ethical framework are put in place.
During a panel discussion that included Anthropic co-founder JackClark, Georgieva said AI was already strengthening the global economy, but could also deliver negative shocks if it failed to deliver major productivity gains as quickly as hoped, Reuters reports.
Georgieva says:
“If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities. And above all, we do need an ethical foundation, and I’m not sure we are there as a society.”
The pound has touched its highest level against the US dollar in over three weeks.
Sterling has gained half a cent to $1.3335, its highest level since 23 September.
Traders are expecting the Bank of England to raise interest rates in November – higher rates are typically good for a currency’s value.
Investors will also be weighing up the impact of the budget later this month – and wondering whether John Healey will maintain the UK’s fiscal headroom – the buffer for meeting its borrowing rules.
Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at global financial services firm and FX specialists Ebury, says:
“The question that matters most to us is how the budget could affect the pound and the gilt market.
We see the fallout in markets as dependent on whether Healey can keep the economic damage to a minimum, while convincing markets that future spending plans won’t come at the expense of debt sustainability.”
Pensioners could suffer if the government hikes taxes on banks, points out Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell:
“The government might argue that banks are doling out significant amounts of money in dividends to shareholders, implying there is plenty of scope for them to pay a little bit more tax. The flipside is that any hit to dividends to offset higher taxes would penalise the large number of people in retirement who invest in banking shares for income.
In other banking news, the UK government reportedly tried to persuade UBS to shift its headquarters and stock market listing to London in the event of the bank relocating out of Switzerland.
Rachel Reeves pitched London as a potential new home for UBS in discussions with the bank’s chair Colm Kelleher during her time as chancellor, according to people briefed on the talks.
The pair discussed the possibility of UBS moving its legal headquarters and listing to the UK if it were to redomicile, the people added, with the most recent meeting taking place earlier this year.
Will Howlett, financials analyst at QuilterCheviot, points out that the jump in bank profits means tehy can absorb higher taxes.
He also suggests that higher bank taxes are already ‘priced in’ to the company’s share prices, saying:
“With the runup to the Budget and the rumour mongering that comes with it now in full flow, the government seems to be giving the UK’s banking sector some mixed messages. John Healey has called the UK’s banks a ‘jewel in the crown of the economy’, yet briefings suggest they are going to get hit by a fresh increase in the levy on its profits.
“The banks did manage to escape such measures last year, but with higher interest rates now expected for longer, the government may be thinking now is the time they can strike, especially if they want to limit the number of personal taxes they go after at the budget. The government is facing increased fiscal pressure as a result of the Middle East shock, and while economic growth is solid just now, this would appear easier pickings to help bolster the public finances.
“That said, much of this is reflected in valuations, with UK domestic banks already trading at a discount to European peers. That may explain the relatively muted reaction to share prices this morning. More domestically focused banks, like Lloyds and NatWest have seen drops in their share prices of around 2%, although this is far smaller than the approximately 6% hit you would see if the surcharge were raised by 5 percentage points back to the 8% where it stood previously. Much of the bad news is already priced in at a time where the banks are also able to absorb such a hit thanks to the profits they are making at the moment as a result of higher interest rates.
Worst week for South Korea's stock market since the financial crisis
Elsewhere in the markets today, South Korea’s Kospi share index has recorded its biggest weekly loss since October 2008, down 14.5% this week.
Although the Kospi did rise today (+2%), it was still a bad week for technology stocks – as investors worried about the borrowing, spending commitments and future profitability of AI companies.
The reality is that while companies embraced AI aggressively as it first emerged, now they are figuring out how to use it effectively while keeping AI costs under control. A slowing, more careful, path towards corporate adoption has been missed by the market which remained wildly frothy about valuations.
British banking stocks have eased following last night’s reports that John Healey will tax the banks in the budget, says Angeline Ong, senior technical analyst at investing and trading platform IG
“A UK bank tax risk is now a base case. If it is confirmed on 28 October, it’ll be the size and timing that will be key.
If Healey does go ahead, shares of Lloyds and NatWest, which are almost entirely exposed to the UK, would likely be impacted most, and you are seeing this already in the share price reaction today. Barclays is partly exposed. HSBC is least exposed in the mix.”
Expectations of a budget tax raid aren’t the only thing weighing on Lloyds’ share price this morning.
The bank has also been hit with a broker downgrade – RBC cut its target price for Lloyds this morning, citing increased competition in the UK deposit market.
Shares in UK banks are dropping at the start of trading, as investors react to the Guardian’s scoop that John Healey is poised to increase taxes on Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget.
Lloyds Banking Group are the top faller on the FTSE 100, down around 1.9%, with NatWest dropping by 1.6%.
BoE's Bailey: seeing 'quite subdued' evidence of second round inflation effects
Heather Stewart
Elsewhere in Bangkok today, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey, was interviewed at the Institute of International Finance annual members’ meeting, being held across town in Bangkok.
With the BoE’s monetary policy committee due to set interest rates in three weeks’ time, Bailey said he was not yet seeing many signs of the “second round effects,” that would indicate inflation has spread beyond the energy sector.
Bailey said:
“I think it’s too early, but to the extent we’ve seen evidence, so far it’s been quite subdued.”
Warsh: Super intelligence driving 'massive investment surge'
Heather Stewart
Heather Stewart is the Guardian’s economic editor, reporting from Thailand.
US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent hasn’t bothered to show up in Bangkok this week for the IMF/World Bank annual meetings, but Federal Reserve chairman KevinWarsh is here.
He appeared on stage earlier today in a “fireside chat” with an old friend: the IMF’s managing director - KristalinaGeorgieva.
Aside from lavishing praise on Warsh, Georgieva asked him about the potential economic impact of AI.
He said AI - for which he used Donald Trump’s preferred term, “Super Intelligence,” is, “probably the most consequential change to the US and the global economy in my lifetime to this point,” which is causing a “massive investment surge”.
Eventually, he said it will boost productivity - “there really is, I think a huge benefit to the global economy, to the US economy over the horizon.” But - with inflation rising sharply in the US - he said there are likely to be short-term bumps in the road.
“If you believe, like I believe, that it will make economies and countries that put it to good use, more productive, that it’s going to make it so that we will have more wealth, then that has to be a very good thing. But the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one.”
Echoing the IMF’s warnings earlier this week about the potential for an AI-led market correction, Warsh added, “we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies. Who’s going to get to make the money? What are the consequences for those that bet that they were going to make money, but the market structure doesn’t allow it?” He said his attitude was one of optimism, leavened by seriousness.
In terms of the short-term outlook, it was not surprising given his rejection of “forward guidance,” that Warsh declined to give any sense of where interest rates might go, after last month’s increase. “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” he said - prompting Georgieva to joke that he had disappointed half the audience.
CBI: Chancellor should avoid 'further sector-specific taxation'
The Confederation of British Industry has suggested John Healey should avoid “further sector-specific taxation”, such as a bank tax.
LouiseHellem, chief economist at the CBI, said:
“The financial services sector is vital to driving investment, innovation and business growth across the economy. Government has set the right direction through its Financial Services Growth and Competitiveness Strategy and the Leeds Reforms – the priority now is delivery.
“The autumn Budget should set the agenda for a competitive and predictable environment that turns those reforms into tangible progress, unlocking domestic investment, deepening UK capital markets and helping more firms to scale and grow.
“It should also avoid measures that would undermine competitiveness or weaken incentives to invest. With the business tax contribution already at a record share of receipts, that means avoiding further sector-specific taxation, including on a banking sector already facing a higher tax rate than competing international financial centres.”
